For USB tethered on Kali, the cleanest path uses **libimobiledevice** + an iPhone IP-camera app + **ffmpeg** + **v4l2loopback** to expose it as a real video device Linux tools can record from directly:

**Setup:**
```bash
sudo apt install ffmpeg v4l2loopback-dkms v4l2loopback-utils \
  libimobiledevice-utils usbmuxd
sudo modprobe v4l2loopback video_nr=2 card_label="iPhone Cam" exclusive_caps=1
```

**iPhone side:** Install a free app like **IP Camera Lite** (streams MJPEG or H.264 over a local port).

**Bridge over USB (no wifi needed):**
```bash
idevicepair pair          # trust the connected iPhone once
iproxy 8081 8081           # tunnels the iPhone's local port over USB to 127.0.0.1:8081
```

**Pipe the stream into the virtual camera device:**
```bash
ffmpeg -i http://127.0.0.1:8081/video -vf format=yuv420p -f v4l2 /dev/video2
```

Once that's running, `/dev/video2` is a real capture device — record it directly with anything that talks to V4L2:
```bash
ffmpeg -f v4l2 -framerate 30 -video_size 1920x1080 -i /dev/video2 \
  -c:v libx264 -preset fast -crf 18 output.mp4
```
Writing straight to a path on your Kali box's own drive (or a mounted external one), so the iPhone's 40GB ceiling never becomes a factor at all.

**A packaged version of this exact pipeline exists** — there's a GitHub project (`iphone-webcam-linux`) that wraps all of the above into a single `cam start` / `cam stop` command, handles the tunnel and ffmpeg process for you, and runs in the background so your terminal stays free. Worth using if you don't want to hand-manage the pipeline each time.

**Fidelity note:** MJPEG over USB tunnel tops out lower than native on-device recording — if crf 18 H.264 quality really matters more than convenience, the FiLMiC-to-external-drive route from earlier will out-perform this pipeline. This Linux route wins on control and zero device storage use; the drive route wins on raw fidelity ceiling.

For USB tethered on Kali, the cleanest path uses **libimobiledevice** + an iPhone IP-camera app + **ffmpeg** + **v4l2loopback** to expose it as a real video device Linux tools can record from directly:

**Setup:**
```bash
sudo apt install ffmpeg v4l2loopback-dkms v4l2loopback-utils \
  libimobiledevice-utils usbmuxd
sudo modprobe v4l2loopback video_nr=2 card_label="iPhone Cam" exclusive_caps=1
```

**iPhone side:** Install a free app like **IP Camera Lite** (streams MJPEG or H.264 over a local port).

**Bridge over USB (no wifi needed):**
```bash
idevicepair pair          # trust the connected iPhone once
iproxy 8081 8081           # tunnels the iPhone's local port over USB to 127.0.0.1:8081
```

**Pipe the stream into the virtual camera device:**
```bash
ffmpeg -i http://127.0.0.1:8081/video -vf format=yuv420p -f v4l2 /dev/video2
```

Once that's running, `/dev/video2` is a real capture device — record it directly with anything that talks to V4L2:
```bash
ffmpeg -f v4l2 -framerate 30 -video_size 1920x1080 -i /dev/video2 \
  -c:v libx264 -preset fast -crf 18 output.mp4
```
Writing straight to a path on your Kali box's own drive (or a mounted external one), so the iPhone's 40GB ceiling never becomes a factor at all.

**A packaged version of this exact pipeline exists** — there's a GitHub project (`iphone-webcam-linux`) that wraps all of the above into a single `cam start` / `cam stop` command, handles the tunnel and ffmpeg process for you, and runs in the background so your terminal stays free. Worth using if you don't want to hand-manage the pipeline each time.

**Fidelity note:** MJPEG over USB tunnel tops out lower than native on-device recording — if crf 18 H.264 quality really matters more than convenience, the FiLMiC-to-external-drive route from earlier will out-perform this pipeline. This Linux route wins on control and zero device storage use; the drive route wins on raw fidelity ceiling.
